summary: Describes the operational convention of placing certain DNS records under a reserved node name that begins with an underscore, such as _name, beneath the domain they apply to. It sets up an IANA registry for these names so uses do not collide. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Some services put their notes in special DNS folders whose names start with an underscore. This document sets up a shared list so two services do not pick the same folder name.

subtitle: How DNS names that start with an underscore scope a record to its parent domain, and the IANA registry that keeps them from colliding.

tldr.problem: The DNS lets any record type sit under any name, so services that reuse generic types such as TXT, SRV and URI have no clean way to separate one use from another, and independent uses of the same underscored name could collide.
tldr.mechanism: Records are placed under a reserved node name that begins with an underscore, beneath the domain they apply to. The underscored name closest to the root is recorded in a new IANA registry, paired with the record type.
tldr.outcome: A lookup of the underscored name returns only the relevant records, and the registry avoids name collisions. The RFC is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Registry
facts.value: Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names

today: RFC 8552 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 222) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. The registry it creates is the place where global underscored node names are recorded, and the companion document is RFC 8553.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs Scoped Names
sections.content:
The core DNS specifications, RFC 1035 and RFC 2181, assign no meaning to domain names or their parts. They also put no limits on which resource record (RR) types can be stored under which names. A name such as www or ftp may suggest a service, but that is an operational habit, not protocol meaning.

Adding a new RR type has proven extremely challenging, with significant adoption and use barriers. So some service designers reuse an existing type and restrict where it may appear. That restriction is the idea this RFC describes and formalizes.
sections.eli5: The DNS lets you put any kind of note under any name, so notes for different jobs get mixed up. Making a brand new kind of note is slow and hard, so people look for a tidier trick.

sections.title: Underscore-Based Scoping
sections.content:
Instead of defining a new RR type, a service can use an existing type but place it in a scoped leaf. Scope here is a static property of the DNS name, not something that depends on the query. The leaf sits in a branch under the parent domain that the data applies to, and the branch is marked by one or more reserved node names. At least the first (highest) of them begins with an underscore, such as _name.

Host names cannot contain an underscore (RFC 952), so an underscored name can never be confused with a legal host name. The result is a space for "attributes", in the form of RR types, that belong to the parent domain. For example, _domainkey.example. is an attribute of example.. DKIM (RFC 6376) uses _domainkey to hold a TXT record with signing information for the parent domain.

This helps most with general-purpose types: TXT, SRV and URI. Without scoping, a client gets back an undifferentiated mass of these records and must parse them to find the relevant ones, and sometimes the result is ambiguous. With scoping, only the relevant RRsets are returned.
sections.eli5: Think of putting a labeled folder inside a bigger folder. A folder named with an underscore can only be a special folder, never a normal name. When you open it, you find only the papers meant for that one job.

sections.title: Scaling and Global Names
sections.content:
Some RR types cause scaling problems if the whole RRset for a name is collected in one leaf. The alternative described here puts the RRset under a specially named branch, so it lives at _branch.domain-name.example rather than at domain-name.example. A direct lookup of that subordinate leaf returns only the desired record types, at no greater cost than a typical DNS lookup.

A domain name can have several node names that begin with an underscore. The one closest to the root, the topmost, is the global underscored node name. In the usual presentation of a name, this is the rightmost underscored label. Names lower down are handled within the scope of the global one.
sections.eli5: A lookup can go straight to the one small folder you need instead of dumping out the whole cabinet. The folder name closest to the top of the cabinet is the one that must be unique across everyone.

sections.title: History and Wildcard Problems
sections.content:
Different uses of underscored names grew up without coordination. TXT records have no consistent internal syntax for telling uses apart. The SRV (RFC 2782) and URI (RFC 7553) records were designed to distinguish uses, and act as templates that need a further specification for each application. SRV names come from two levels: a lower-level _service and an upper-level _proto, whose pool of names was not explicitly defined.

The combined effect was a long list of uncoordinated reserved names, which invites an eventual name-assignment collision. The remedy is this document and a companion, RFC 8553, which define the registry and try to register names already in use.

DNS wildcards also interact poorly with underscored names. Wildcards apply only to leaf names, so there is no equivalent of a wildcard for prefixed names; label.*.example.com is not a wildcard. Conversely, *.example.com can match an underscored name and return a record of the controlled type that was never meant for that context.
sections.eli5: For a long time, many groups made up their own special folder names without checking with each other, so two could have picked the same one. The fix is a shared list. Also, the catch-all trick in DNS can accidentally hand out the wrong thing from a special folder.

sections.title: The Underscored Node Names Registry
sections.content:
The "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry exists to avoid collisions when the same underscored name is used for different applications. The rule is: if a public specification calls for an underscored node name, the global one, closest to the DNS root, MUST be entered in the registry.

Only global names are listed. As the RFC's example, from names like _service1, _protoB._service2 and _protoE._region._authority, the registry would list _service1, _service2, _service3, _service4 and _authority. Each registered global name owns a distinct subordinate namespace, and the specification that creates the entry is responsible for defining and registering the lower-level names. Other RRsets that are not part of the scope MAY still be used in an underscore-scoped leaf.

Each entry has three fields: the RR Type, the _NODE NAME (recorded in lowercase) and a Reference to the specification. The combination of RR Type and name MUST be unique, and every RR type used with a name needs its own entry. The organization producing the referenced specification keeps control over the entry. Section 3 gives specification writers a template: "Per RFC 8552, please add the following entry to the registry".
sections.eli5: The shared list has three columns: what kind of note, which folder name, and who wrote the rules. The same pair can only appear once, and the folder name is always written in small letters so people compare names the same way.

sections.title: Initial Entries and Expert Review
sections.content:
The registry starts with entries drawn from existing specifications. Examples in the RFC's table include TXT with _dmarc, _domainkey, _spf and _acme-challenge; TLSA with _tcp and _udp; SRV with _tcp, _udp and _sip; and many URI entries from RFC 6118. Two are special. The NULL entry _ta-* means every name that begins with the string _ta-, and does not refer to a DNS wildcard. The name _example is reserved across all RRsets.

New entries use Expert Review. The review only checks that the details for the entry are sufficiently clear, precise and complete, and that the combination of underscored name and RR type is unique in the table. Other questions of technical quality are out of scope.

The RFC also adds a note to the "Enumservice Registrations" registry: when adding an entry there, strong consideration should be given to also adding one to the underscored-names registry.
sections.eli5: The list started with names people were already using. When someone asks to add a new one, a reviewer only checks that the request is clear and that nobody else has the same pair, not whether the idea is a good one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is a single sentence: this memo raises no security issues. The related risk worth noting from the body of the text is the wildcard interaction above, where a wildcard record can match an underscored name and return data that does not follow that name's rules.
sections.eli5: The authors say this list does not add new dangers. The only trap they point out is that a catch-all entry might answer for a special folder by mistake.
